title: Optimize walkthrough — KV prefetch economics & batching deep dive with LunarByte
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked LunarByte through Optimize recommendations: prefix/KV prefetch patterns, batching/concurrency settings and a small cost model for their chat-heavy product. Customer is evaluating Dedicated capacity but wants hosted pilot results and security artifacts. Agreed to run a short pilot benchmark with 1M tokens workload and share tuned config & estimated savings.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62m
Recording ID: fb-20250729-0115-lunarbyte
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (LunarByte Head ML), Marcus (SRE), Elena (CTO), Samir (Data Eng)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros, Diego will run the optimize walkthrough, I’ll kick off and keep time.
[00:18] Priya: Hi, Priya here, thanks. We asked specifically about KV prefetch and batching because our product has a lot of short-lived chat sessions — lots of repeated prefixes.
[00:28] Diego: Great, that’s exactly the scenario where prefix/KV caching and prefetch shine. Quick show of hands — are you running current generation models, or do you expect to use a quantized variant for cost?
[00:38] Marcus: We’d like to start with an open model quantized to int8 on Dedicated, but for a pilot we can use hosted to baseline.
[00:45] Diego: Perfect. I’ll walk through three things: 1) prefix cache mechanics (we call it KV cache), 2) prefetch rules and heuristics, 3) a micro cost model for your traffic pattern.
[00:55] Speaker 1: (mumble) sorry can you repeat prefet—
[01:02] Diego: Yeah, prefetching — pre-computing the KV state for high-frequency prefixes so subsequent requests skip early token compute.
[01:10] Samir: How is that different from just caching full responses? We already have response-level CDN caches for static prompts.
[01:18] Diego: Good question. Response CDN helps for exact-match responses. Prefix/KV cache is agnostic to the final output; it stores the model's key/value memory after processing the static prefix. So for dynamic tails you get full model behavior but avoid reprocessing the prefix each time.
[01:34] Priya: In our case the first 40 tokens are identical across 70% of sessions; that seems high.
[01:40] Diego: That’s ideal. In our sample math, if you can avoid redoing those 40 tokens per request, compute drops significantly.
[01:46] [02:10] Diego: Slide — cost model scenario: assume 10k requests/day, avg tail 60 tokens, prefix 40 tokens. Baseline (no KV, no batching) does full 100 token compute per request. With KV prefetch + prefix cache, prefix compute eliminated for cached sessions — roughly saves 40% of per-request compute for cached ones. Combine with batching (average batch size 6) and you can push compute savings to 45–55% depending on sequence lengths and concurrency.
[03:05] Marcus: Can you walk numbers with concurrency? Our peak QPS is ~5 rps with spiky bursts.
[03:12] Diego: Sure. With 5 QPS and batching window of 20–30ms you get effective batch sizes of 4–8 (depends on traffic shape). Our console sim shows at 5 QPS a 25ms batching delay yields batch size ~5 and tail latency still sub-120ms for token streaming. If you want strict p99 < 200ms, we recommend batching window 15–20ms and aggressive prefetch for the top 10 prefixes.
[03:40] Elena: Is the prefetch synchronous? I.e., do you do it on session start or periodically?
[03:45] Diego: Two modes: on-demand prefetch on session start for known prefixes, or asynchronous prefetch warmed by predicted sessions. For LunarByte we recommend hybrid: warm top-100 prefixes asynchronously after deployment, and on-demand prefetch for new prefixes.
[04:02] Priya: What about cache eviction and memory on the GPU? We are worried about memory footprint if we hold many KV states.
[04:10] Diego: Right — KV states are proportional to sequence length and number of layers. Our console shows memory per prefix is small (a few MB) for 6k context models, but totals add up. For Dedicated we suggest a KV LRU with soft eviction + compression (quantized KV) which we offer in Redwood Optimize configs. Also, you can tier cache: keep hot prefixes on-GPU, warm prefixes in host RAM.
[04:36] Speaker 2: (unclear) lru will drop but...
[04:42] Diego: Yeah, sorry transcription — LRU eviction with TTL.
[04:45] [07:00] Diego: Demo: I’m switching to the console — this is the Optimize tab. Here you can see a suggested policy: prefetch top-10 prefixes, batch window 25ms, concurrent streams 8, fallback to smaller model when latency increases. You can toggle simulated traffic and it runs the cost sim.
[07:28] Priya: Can you share the sim? Our finance folks want a conservative number.
[07:33] Diego: Absolutely — we’ll export the spreadsheet. In the sim for your traffic shape the hosted pilot shows estimated unit compute cost reduction from baseline by ~48% and end-to-end token cost reduction ~38% after applying network and storage overhead.
[07:52] Marcus: Those look good — but what about cold-starts? If a prefix is not in cache we pay full compute and also a prefetch cost, right?
[07:59] Diego: Correct. Cold prefixes incur full compute; however, you amortize by keeping hot prefixes cached. The sim models a cache hit rate; if your hit rate drops below ~20% then the economics shift and batching becomes dominant savings.
[08:15] Priya: SLOs — can we still meet our p95 latency target of 350ms when we enable batching and prefetching?
[08:22] Diego: Yes — our recommendations are conservative: small batching windows, prefer prefetch for hot prefixes, and immediate fallback to smaller model variants for p95-sensitive routes. You can also pin specific routes to bypass batching.
[08:35] [11:50] Sofia: Security questions — Marcus, I think you had SOC 2 and KMS needs?
[11:55] Marcus: Yes, and we need audit logs per token and encryption-at-rest with BYOK (bring your own key) support. Also, can Redwood run in our VPC?
[12:05] Diego: For security artifacts we’ll send the SOC 2 summary, KMS integration guide and the private deployment checklist. Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem — for BYOK we support KMS integrations and HSM workflows. For audit logs we emit request/response metadata and token counts; we don’t store raw customer data unless configured.
[12:25] Priya: Does the hosted pilot require us to send raw prompts to Redwood? We prefer redaction options.
[12:31] Diego: We have automatic PII redaction options and route-level masking in the console. For strict regulatory scenarios we advise Private.
[12:40] [18:12] Diego: Back to cost numbers — example: 10k daily requests, baseline 100 tokens => 1M tokens/day. If 70% have cached prefix and prefetch avoids 40 tokens per cached request, that’s 280k tokens saved/day (~28%). With batching savings on top you get to ~45% compute reduction. If your monthly token volume is 30M, that’s roughly X (placeholder) compute-hours saved; I’ll attach the full calcs.
[18:48] Samir: Can you run a one-week AB test? We want to validate quality regression risk when using prefetch + batching.
[18:56] Diego: Yes — recommended pilot: 1-week hosted pilot with 10% traffic routed to Redwood Optimize config, and the rest to your baseline. We collect quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE not ideal for chat — we'll use custom eval prompts and human spot checks).
[19:12] Priya: How do you flag generation regressions introduced by batching?
[19:18] Diego: Two ways: conditional rollout + automated quality monitors in Optimize tied to prompt sets. If model outputs diverge from baseline beyond threshold, system triggers rollback. We’ll show how to set thresholds in the dashboard.
[19:32] [27:05] Diego: Live config example — policy yaml: prefetch: top_prefixes: 50; batch_window_ms: 25; max_batch: 16; fallback_model: smaller-quantized. You can tweak by route.
[27:40] Priya: That yaml — does console generate it or we write?
[27:44] Diego: Console generates recommended yaml which you can edit. We support CLI and API updates too.
[28:05] Elena: On Dedicated, does the cost model change? We’re looking at a committed pool for predictable throughput.
[28:13] Diego: On Dedicated the per-token compute cost is lower (committed GPU hours), and caching efficiency is higher because you control memory and warmers. Our sim for Dedicated typically shows higher absolute savings because you can pin hot KV to GPU and avoid cross-tenant noise. We’ll model both hosted pilot and a 6-month Dedicated commit for you.
[28:40] Marcus: Any performance caveats for long-context models? We use 32k context for some workflows.
[28:48] Diego: Long context increases KV memory footprint; cache per prefix is larger. Prefetch still helps but you need larger GPU RAM or more aggressive tiering. Optimize can auto-suggest quantized KV and TTLs to keep memory within budget.
[29:05] [35:00] Sofia: Recap and next steps. Diego, can you list what you’ll share?
[35:06] Diego: Sure — 1) exported cost sim spreadsheet for LunarByte traffic, 2) sample Optimize policy yaml, 3) SOC2/KMS security doc links, 4) pilot runbook for a one-week AB test, 5) data for Dedicated capacity estimate.
[35:20] Priya: Helpful. Also please include suggested eval prompts and the divergence threshold examples.
[35:27] Diego: Will do.
[35:35] [50:10] Priya: One last thing — what’s a realistic timeline from pilot to Dedicated for us?
[50:18] Sofia: Typically pilot 1–2 weeks, analysis 1 week, then Dedicated procurement 4–8 weeks depending on legal and network setup. For BYOK + VPC there’s an extra 2–3 weeks for onboarding.
[50:32] Elena: Can we get a price ballpark for a 3-month committed Dedicated?
[50:38] Sofia: We’ll do a preliminary commit estimate in the spreadsheet; final pricing requires a usage profile but expect discounts vs hosted per token.
[50:48] [60:00] Sofia: Thanks everyone. We’ll email the artifacts and schedule the kickoff for the pilot.

End transcript.
